sources.title: Statistical Analysis of the Indus Script Using n-Grams
sources.access: Opened publisher full text through web; downloaded publisher HTML locally.
locations: Model Performance Evaluation by Cross-Validation, paragraphs 1–3
sources.observations: EBUDS retains one instance per repeated text and has 1,548 texts. Five 80:20 folds and 100 random deletion repetitions per fold yield 74% sensitivity in the 90% cumulative-probability candidate set. This is not exact top-one accuracy.
sources.rights_notice: Publisher states Creative Commons Attribution; raw witness stays local.

sources.title: A Markov model of the Indus script
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 106(33): 13685–13690
sources.access: Opened and downloaded author-hosted PDF, including supplement.
locations: PDF page 4, Filling in Incomplete Indus Inscriptions
PDF pages 6–10, methods and supporting information
sources.observations: Markov missing-sign prediction is established prior work. The paper's roughly 74% statement points to the cross-validation study detailed by Yadav et al.; its candidate-set criterion should not be treated as this package's exact first-guess outcome.

sources.title: Statistical models for identifying missing and unclear signs of the Indus script
sources.venue: Journal of Emerging Investigators 6, published 7 July 2023, PDF pages 1–8
sources.access: Opened publisher abstract and full PDF; downloaded full PDF locally.
locations: PDF pages 4–5, Missing signs in the Test dataset and predictions
sources.observations: The body reports about 35% exact sign match, 57% top-five and 63% top-ten. It uses 2,223 unique texts, an 80:20 split and 100 random single-sign deletion repetitions, with n-gram choices discussed using the test set. The abstract's 63% is not exact top-one.
sources.rights_notice: Publisher states attribution non-commercial no-derivatives. Download remains local.

sources.title: Statistical Structure in Indus Sign Sequences
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 6th International Conference on Natural Language Processing for the Digital Humanities, pages 314–319
sources.access: Opened ACL record and full PDF; downloaded full PDF locally.
sources.observations: Reports 6,579 inscriptions and an object-type-stratified 80:20 split. A BiLSTM next-token assay reports real-test perplexity 2.60 and synthetic sequence comparisons. These are different queries and outcome definitions from known-slot restoration; no object-component split is specified in the opened methods.

sources.title: Restoring and attributing ancient texts using deep neural networks
sources.access: Opened PMC full text through web. Direct local HTTP acquisition returned a reCAPTCHA page rather than the article; retained as a failed witness.
sources.observations: Removes 9,441 duplicate texts; I.PHI has 78,608 inscriptions and identifier-ending validation/test splits. Eight transformer blocks predict restoration and attribution. Artificially hides spans of 1–10 characters, reporting 61.8% top-one restoration and 26.3% character error rate. Those spans and alphabet differ from single Indus-code masks.
sources.rights_notice: Opened article states CC BY 4.0, with third-party exclusions where credited.

sources.title: Contextualizing ancient texts with generative neural networks
sources.access: Publisher search result and PubMed bibliographic record opened. Publisher and PMC full-text routes failed. Downloaded and read the Warwick author PDF locally with page-indexed extraction.
locations: Author PDF page 8, LED dataset preparation and partitioning
sources.observations: Deduplicates by Trismegistos identities and more than 90% fuzzy content similarity, then partitions by identifier endings. Latin fixed-length restoration reports 40.5% character error rate and 46.5% top-20 accuracy; its unknown-length task has different outcomes. Its multimodal context retrieval is beyond this package's small masked-slot networks.

sources.title: Restoring Mycenaean Linear B ‘A&B’ series tablets using supervised and transfer learning
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Machine Learning for Ancient Languages, pages 115–129
sources.access: Opened ACL record and full PDF; downloaded and extracted locally.
sources.observations: On 426 A&B sequences using leave-one-out prediction, the bidirectional recurrent model achieves 30.28% top-one, 50.23% top-five and 57.75% top-ten. Transfer from D gives 25.65% or 24.71% top-one, with no overall improvement in the synthetic gap assay. Script, selection and gap distribution differ from this benchmark.

sources.title: An Empirical Study of Smoothing Techniques for Language Modeling
sources.venue: Harvard University Computer Science Group, Technical Report TR-10-98
sources.access: Opened Microsoft-hosted author report; downloaded and extracted locally.
sources.observations: Modified Kneser–Ney uses different discounts for singleton, doubleton and 3+ counts; count-of-count formulas estimate them. This package adds explicit sparse-count clipping, a discount-scale grid and a finite-vocabulary bottom floor.
